review.credibility_reason: Upstream official docs, checked line by line against the v0.33.0 source for flags and defaults. Example numbers in the docs are illustrative outputs on unspecified hardware and are not usable as performance data.
review.summary: The index page links to the Benchmark CLI (vllm bench serve / throughput / latency / forward / startup), Parameter Sweeps (vllm bench sweep serve, serve_workload, startup, plot) and the CI dashboard. vllm bench serve is a client that load-tests any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and reports throughput, TTFT, TPOT, ITL and optionally E2EL, with a configurable request rate, burstiness, concurrency cap and percentiles. The docs say vllm bench serve is mainly for feature and regression testing, and they recommend GuideLLM for benchmarking production servers. The docs do not cover Docker. From the v0.33.0 Dockerfile, the vllm-openai image has ENTRYPOINT ["vllm","serve"], WORKDIR /vllm-workspace and a copy of benchmarks/, so a client run needs --entrypoint vllm. bench latency and bench throughput are offline: they load the model in-process. On a 16 GB GPU they cannot run beside a running server. For an agent workload, the docs offer BFCL tool-calling traffic, prefix_repetition, timed trace replay, the long-document-QA and prefix-caching scripts, and benchmarks/multi_turn. They warn that repeated runs inflate throughput through the prefix cache.

findings.claim: Measured at the client. TTFT runs from sending the request to the first streamed output. ITL is the gap between consecutive streamed outputs, aggregated over all requests. TPOT = (E2E latency - TTFT) / (output tokens - 1), computed per request and then aggregated. With speculative decoding, ITL undercounts tokens per gap, so compare TPOT across runs, not ITL. The summary reports request throughput, output token throughput and total token throughput.

Allowed metrics are ttft, tpot, itl, e2el, client_queue_time and e2el_including_client_queue. The default is ttft,tpot,itl for generative models. --metric-percentiles defaults to "99"; pass for example 50,90,99. --goodput takes KEY:VALUE SLOs in ms for ttft, tpot and e2el.

--request-rate defaults to inf, which sends all requests at t=0. A finite rate uses Poisson arrivals (--burstiness 1.0) or a Gamma distribution, and burstiness has no effect at inf. --max-concurrency defaults to unlimited. The docs call --request-rate inf with a concurrency limit the most common configuration. Ramp-up uses --ramp-up-strategy linear|exponential with --ramp-up-start-rps and --ramp-up-end-rps. --num-warmups defaults to 0.

Repeating vllm bench serve against the same server can reuse prompts left in the prefix cache and inflate throughput. The random dataset is reproducible because --seed defaults to 0. Vary --seed, reset or restart the server, or use vllm bench sweep serve, which calls the /reset_*_cache endpoints between runs.

At startup vLLM logs 'GPU KV cache size: N tokens' and 'Maximum concurrency for X tokens per request'. max_concurrency = kv_cache_size / max_model_len. For capacity tests, set --max-concurrency to 80-90% of that figure.

The BFCL dataset (--dataset-name hf --dataset-path gorilla-llm/Berkeley-Function-Calling-Leaderboard --bfcl-categories simple,live_simple,multiple) sends a per-sample tools schema and chat history through openai-chat. The server needs --enable-auto-tool-choice and a --tool-call-parser. Multi-turn BFCL categories are not supported.

Reasoning deltas count toward TTFT and ITL, and only output text counts as generated text. Do not pass --extra-body '{"include_reasoning": false}' for reasoning models: the reasoning phase is then absorbed into TTFT.

Several tools are available. prefix_repetition (--prefix-repetition-prefix-len/-suffix-len/-num-prefixes/-output-len) models shared system prompts. timed_trace replays Mooncake conversation traces (--self-timed, --timed-trace-sec-multiplier). benchmarks/benchmark_long_document_qa_throughput.py and benchmarks/benchmark_prefix_caching.py are offline scripts. benchmarks/multi_turn/benchmark_serving_multi_turn.py runs synthetic multi-turn chats against a server (--num-clients, --max-active-conversations) and has its own requirements.txt.

--save-result writes JSON (default name {label}-{request_rate}qps-{model}-{datetime}.json; set --result-dir and --result-filename). --save-detailed adds per-request ttfts, itls and errors. --metadata k=v records the configuration. --plot-timeline writes an HTML timeline, colored by --timeline-itl-thresholds (default 25,50 ms). --plot-dataset-stats writes a matplotlib figure.

With the server started with --enable-per-request-metrics, --save-detailed also stores server_queue_times and server_ttfts. TTFT is approximately server_queue_time + server_ttft + frontend/network overhead. The docs say this adds CPU overhead, so use it for diagnostic runs only.

vllm bench sweep serve --serve-cmd '...' --bench-cmd '...' --serve-params serve.json --bench-params bench.json --output-dir DIR --experiment-name NAME starts the server itself and runs the Cartesian product, with 3 runs per combination by default (--num-runs). It also takes --warmup-num-prompts, --dry-run, --resume and --continue-on-error. vllm bench sweep serve_workload sweeps --workload-var request_rate (default) or max_concurrency, and the docs call max_concurrency more reliable. vllm bench sweep plot DIR --var-x max_concurrency --var-y median_ttft_ms|total_token_throughput draws the curves. vllm bench sweep startup compares cold and warm start times.

vllm bench throughput --model M --dataset-name random --random-input-len 500 --random-output-len 150 --num-prompts 10 loads the model in-process (backends vllm, hf, mii, vllm-chat). It needs the GPU to itself.

vllm bench latency is not described in the benchmarking docs. In source, its defaults are --input-len 32, --output-len 128, --batch-size 8, --num-iters-warmup 10, --num-iters 30, and --output-json. It is offline: it loads the model in-process and measures batch latency.

The docs do not cover Docker. The v0.33.0 Dockerfile sets ENTRYPOINT ["vllm","serve"] and WORKDIR /vllm-workspace and copies examples/ and benchmarks/, so a client run must override the entrypoint: docker run --rm --network host --entrypoint vllm vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0 bench serve .... The bench extra in setup.py (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, datasets, scipy, plotly) is optional, and the Dockerfile has no visible install of it. hf datasets, plots and sweep plot may need it. This is unverified because the image is not local.

The client loads a tokenizer for --model, or for --tokenizer if given, to count tokens and build random prompts. Inside a container, mount the HF cache or the model directory, or pass --tokenizer <local path>. --served-model-name sets the API model name when it differs from the tokenizer path.

The docs recommend GuideLLM (github.com/vllm-project/guidellm) for benchmarking production servers, as more flexible in datasets, request formatting and workload patterns. They say vllm bench is mainly for feature and regression testing.

Not documented. Because bench serve speaks plain OpenAI HTTP (openai or openai-chat backend), it should be able to target llama-server's /v1/completions or /v1/chat/completions with --base-url and an HF --tokenizer that matches the GGUF. This would let vLLM and llama.cpp be compared with the same client. It needs a test run.

agreements: Baseline: prefix caching is on by default in v0.33.0. The docs agree, warning that repeated bench serve runs reuse the prefix cache and inflate throughput, so the KB method must vary --seed or reset the cache between runs.

Baseline: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0 is the target image. Its Dockerfile at v0.33.0 ships the benchmarks/ directory and an entrypoint of `vllm serve`, which fits running the client from the same image with --entrypoint vllm.
Baseline parser setup (--enable-auto-tool-choice plus a tool-call parser) is the same precondition the docs give for the BFCL tool-calling benchmark.

kb_notes.note: Benchmark a running server with the client inside the same image: `docker run --rm --network host -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface --entrypoint vllm vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0 bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --model <served-name> --tokenizer <hf-id> --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 512 --ignore-eos --num-prompts 32 --max-concurrency 1 --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --metric-percentiles 50,90,99 --seed $RANDOM --save-result --result-dir /results`. The image's entrypoint is `vllm serve`, so --entrypoint vllm is required (source: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/benchmarking/ and docker/Dockerfile at v0.33.0).

Defaults at v0.33.0 that silently shape results: --num-prompts 1000, --request-rate inf (all requests at t=0), --max-concurrency unlimited, --random-input-len 1024, --random-output-len 128, --random-range-ratio 0.0, --seed 0, --num-warmups 0, --metric-percentiles 99. Always set prompts, concurrency, lengths and seed explicitly (source: vllm/benchmarks/serve.py and datasets.py at v0.33.0).

Prefix caching is on by default, and the random dataset is reproducible for a fixed seed, so a second identical run hits the cache and reports inflated throughput. Change --seed per run, restart the container, or use `vllm bench sweep serve`, which calls the /reset_*_cache endpoints between runs (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/benchmarking/cli/).

For a single-user coding agent, the headline numbers are TTFT at a long prompt (prefill speed) and TPOT at --max-concurrency 1 (decode speed). Run a ladder of --random-input-len 2048, 8192, 32768, 65536 with --max-concurrency 1, then a concurrency sweep of 1, 2, 4 at a fixed length to see how parallel subagents share the GPU.

Metric definitions per the vLLM docs: TTFT runs from request send to the first streamed output; ITL is the gap between streamed outputs; TPOT = (E2EL - TTFT)/(output_tokens - 1) per request. With speculative decoding, compare TPOT rather than ITL, because one streamed chunk can hold several tokens.

Use `--backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions` so the chat template, reasoning parser and tool parser are on the measured path, as they are in OpenCode traffic. For reasoning models, do not pass --extra-body '{"include_reasoning": false}': the reasoning phase then disappears into TTFT.

Tool-calling load test: `vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --dataset-name hf --dataset-path gorilla-llm/Berkeley-Function-Calling-Leaderboard --bfcl-categories simple,live_simple,multiple --num-prompts 200`. It needs a server with --enable-auto-tool-choice and a tool-call parser. Multi-turn BFCL categories are unsupported, and this measures latency, not tool-call accuracy.

Agent-like shared prompts: --dataset-name prefix_repetition with --prefix-repetition-prefix-len (for example 8000 to mimic a long system prompt and tool schema), --prefix-repetition-suffix-len, --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes and --prefix-repetition-output-len measures prefix-cache benefit. benchmarks/multi_turn/benchmark_serving_multi_turn.py (in the image under /vllm-workspace/benchmarks, with its own requirements.txt) runs multi-turn conversations against a live server.

`vllm bench latency` and `vllm bench throughput` are offline: they load the model inside the benchmark process. On the 16 GB laptop GPU, stop the server first. Do not run them beside a running vLLM or llama.cpp container.

Concurrency ceiling: the server log at startup prints 'GPU KV cache size: N tokens' and 'Maximum concurrency for <max_model_len> tokens per request: X'. The docs give max_concurrency = kv_cache_size / max_model_len and suggest testing at 80-90% of X. Record both lines with every benchmark result.

Parameter sweeps: `vllm bench sweep serve --serve-cmd 'vllm serve ...' --bench-cmd 'vllm bench serve ...' --serve-params serve.json --bench-params bench.json --output-dir results --experiment-name NAME` runs the Cartesian product, 3 runs each by default (--num-runs). `vllm bench sweep serve_workload --workload-var max_concurrency` finds the latency and throughput knee, and `vllm bench sweep plot` draws it. The sweep starts its own `vllm serve`, so run it inside a container started with a shell entrypoint, not against a separately started server.

Save every run with --save-result --save-detailed --metadata gpu=rtx5080-laptop-140W driver=595.99 vllm=0.33.0 model=<id> quant=<q> kv=<dtype> max_model_len=<n>, so results can be compared later. Add --plot-timeline for an HTML per-request timeline.

The example outputs in the vLLM benchmarking docs (for example 382.89 output tok/s for Hermes-3-Llama-3.1-8B on 10 ShareGPT prompts) come from unspecified hardware and versions. They show output format only and must not be quoted as performance data for any GPU.

Candidate for one client across runtimes, not yet tested: vllm bench serve speaks plain OpenAI HTTP, so `--backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --tokenizer <matching HF repo>` should be able to load-test llama-server with the same prompts used for vLLM. Verify that token counts match llama-server's usage block before comparing.

check.summary: I re-fetched the rendered index page (HTTP 200, title 'Benchmark Suites - vLLM', dated August 11, 2026) and the raw v0.33.0 cli.md, sweeps.md, serve.py, datasets.py, latency.py and Dockerfile into $SCRATCH/src/vllm-benchmarking-check/. All 10 load-bearing items checked match verbatim: the defaults, the prefix-cache warning, the KV concurrency formula with the 80-90% guidance, the GuideLLM recommendation, the include_reasoning warning, the bench latency defaults, and the example outputs (382.89 tok/s, 71.54 ms TTFT, 7.91 ms TPOT, 1072.50 output tok/s). The review reports no conflicts with the baseline, and I found none. There are three small corrections. First, the v0.33.0 tag's tagger date is 2026-11-01, not 2026-11-02. Second, the Dockerfile shows 'COPY benchmarks benchmarks' at L1051, but the stage graph does not prove it reaches the published vllm-openai image, and there is also a nonroot variant with its own entrypoint. The '--entrypoint vllm bench serve' recipe is plausible but untested. Third, the docs' example rows should be labelled illustrative rather than 'measured'.
